chunks.title: Guide to Module 1 — The Prehistory of the Dialectical Problem
chunks.bodyMarkdown:
### Primary orientation

Begin with the historical sections of the Stanford Encyclopedia article “Hegel’s Dialectics,” then read selected passages from Kant’s *Critique of Pure Reason* on the antinomies. The purpose is not to complete a survey of ancient and modern philosophy. It is to isolate the problems Hegel inherits: opposition, contradiction, the unconditioned, the relation of thought to objectivity, and the failure of fixed categories.

### Recommended reading anchors

- Plato, *Parmenides*, the hypotheses concerning the One, read selectively.
- Plato, *Sophist*, sections on being, non-being, identity, and difference.
- Aristotle, *Metaphysics*, Book Γ on non-contradiction and Book Θ on actuality and potentiality, selectively.
- Kant, *Critique of Pure Reason*, Transcendental Dialectic, “The Antinomy of Pure Reason.”
- Hegel, *Lectures on the History of Philosophy*, selections on Heraclitus, Plato, Aristotle, Kant, Fichte, and Schelling.

### Reading focus

The ancient texts should be read for the difference between contradiction as refutation and contradiction as a source of positive conceptual development. Kant should be read for the way reason generates opposed conclusions from its own demand for completeness. Hegel accepts that contradiction is systematic but rejects Kant’s restriction of it to reason’s illegitimate use beyond experience.

Fichte and Schelling matter because they transform Kant’s conditions of experience into dynamic principles. Fichte makes determination an act; Schelling seeks an identity of subject and object. Hegel’s objection is that an asserted identity without developed difference remains abstract.

### Principal caution

Do not construct a story in which all earlier philosophy merely waits for Hegel. The course presents Hegel’s inherited problems, not a triumphalist claim that every predecessor was an incomplete Hegelian.

---

chunks.title: Guide to Module 2 — What Hegel Means by Logic
chunks.bodyMarkdown:
### Core Hegel reading

- *Encyclopaedia Logic*, §§19–25.
- *Encyclopaedia Logic*, §§79–83.
- *Science of Logic*, Preface to the First Edition.
- *Science of Logic*, Preface to the Second Edition.
- *Science of Logic*, “General Concept of Logic.”
- *Science of Logic*, “With What Must the Beginning of Science Be Made?”

### Reading focus

In §§19–25, track Hegel’s claim that logic concerns the pure Idea in the element of thought. Avoid translating this immediately into either subjective psychology or a supernatural realm of entities. The issue is the status of thought determinations.

In the *Science of Logic* introduction, note Hegel’s criticism of the ordinary separation between form and content. Traditional logic is treated as a collection of forms indifferent to the material arranged through them. Hegel’s project is to let the forms develop as content.

The section on the beginning should be read slowly. The beginning must be immediate, but it is also justified through the completed system. The circle does not mean that any starting point is acceptable. Pure Being is chosen because every more determinate beginning would presuppose categories not yet developed.

### Supplementary orientation

- Stanford Encyclopedia, “Georg Wilhelm Friedrich Hegel,” sections on the *Science of Logic* and Hegel’s published corpus.
- Stephen Houlgate, *The Opening of Hegel’s Logic*, introductory chapters.
- Robert Pippin, *Hegel’s Realm of Shadows*, introduction, for a contemporary account of logic as a theory of intelligibility.

### Principal caution

Do not use “objective logic” to mean that categories float as objects outside human practices, and do not use “idealism” to mean that Hegel denies material reality. The exact metaphysical status of the categories is a scholarly dispute. The secure starting point is that Hegel rejects the view that logical form is merely an external instrument of a private mind.

---

chunks.title: Guide to Module 3 — The Three Moments of the Logical
chunks.bodyMarkdown:
### Core Hegel reading

- *Encyclopaedia Logic*, §§79–82, including the remarks and carefully identified *Zusätze*.
- *Phenomenology of Spirit*, Preface, especially the discussion of the result, the negative, and determinate negation.
- *Science of Logic*, Introduction, sections on method and the self-movement of content.

### Reading focus

Section 79 explicitly states that understanding, dialectical reason, and speculative reason are moments rather than independent parts. Section 80 presents understanding as fixation of determinations. Section 81 presents dialectic as their self-sublation. Section 82 presents speculative reason as the affirmative result contained in their dissolution.

The crucial phrase is “determinate negation.” The result is not empty Nothing because a particular determination has been negated. The content of the result is shaped by the path of negation.

Read *Aufhebung* with all three senses in view: cancellation, preservation, and elevation. No English occurrence of “sublation” should become a substitute for specifying what is cancelled, what is preserved, and how the content is transformed.

### Lenin supplement

- Lenin, “Plan of Hegel’s Dialectics (Logic).”
- Lenin, “On the Question of Dialectics.”

Read these only after §§79–82. Lenin highlights division of the One, unity of opposites, and the difference between living and dead knowledge. His formulations are powerful but compressed. They should be unfolded through the primary Hegelian sequences rather than used as stand-alone laws.

### Principal caution

The three moments are not thesis, antithesis, and synthesis. The speculative result is not necessarily a middle position. It is the concrete unity generated by the specific content of the opposed determinations.

---

chunks.title: Guide to Module 4 — Being, Nothing, and Becoming
chunks.bodyMarkdown:
### Core Hegel reading

- *Encyclopaedia Logic*, §§84–89.
- *Science of Logic*, “With What Must the Beginning of Science Be Made?”
- *Science of Logic*, Doctrine of Being, Chapter 1: Being, Nothing, Becoming.

### Reading focus

The reading depends upon maintaining the abstraction. Pure Being must not be imagined as the universe, matter, existence, or a divine presence. Pure Nothing must not be imagined as an empty container or the absence of a particular object.

At the level of complete indeterminacy, neither term has content by which it can remain distinct. Yet their intended meanings differ. Becoming names the movement of their unity and distinction.

In the larger *Science of Logic*, read the remarks because Hegel anticipates objections: ordinary thought opposes Nothing to a determinate something; critics introduce concrete examples; Parmenides and Heraclitus are discussed; Jacobi’s attempt to hold pure space, time, or consciousness in abstraction is examined.

### Secondary interpretation

- Stanford Encyclopedia, “Hegel’s Dialectics,” the Being–Nothing–Becoming example.
- Stephen Houlgate, *The Opening of Hegel’s Logic*, chapters on presuppositionlessness and the opening transition.

Houlgate represents a strong “presuppositionless” reading. Other scholars question whether the beginning is as free from presupposition as Hegel claims. The course need not settle that dispute, but it must distinguish reconstructing Hegel’s intended transition from endorsing every premise.

### Lenin supplement

- Lenin, *Conspectus of Hegel’s Science of Logic*, entries on the beginning, Being, Nothing, and Becoming.

Observe which phrases Lenin copies or marks. The annotations are evidence of his reading priorities, not a replacement for the argument.

### Principal caution

The statement “Being and Nothing are the same” is incomplete without “and different,” their vanishing, and Becoming. Quoting the first phrase alone produces a contradiction Hegel himself does not leave unresolved.

---

chunks.title: Guide to Module 5 — Determinate Being, Finitude, and Infinity
Guide to Module 6 — Quantity and Measure
Guide to Module 7 — Essence, Reflection, and Contradiction
chunks.bodyMarkdown:
### Core Hegel reading

- *Encyclopaedia Logic*, §§112–121, followed by the relevant remarks on identity, difference, opposition, and contradiction.
- *Science of Logic*, Doctrine of Essence:
  - The Essential and the Unessential;
  - Semblance;
  - Positing, External, and Determining Reflection;
  - Identity;
  - Difference and Diversity;
  - Opposition;
  - Contradiction.

### Reading focus

The movement from Being to Essence changes the form of dialectic. Categories no longer simply pass into one another. They are reflexive: each is what it is through another determination and through return from that other.

*Schein* requires special attention. It is not simply false appearance. It is immediacy deprived of independent subsistence and retained as a moment within Essence. Reflection is correspondingly not just the activity of a human observer. It is the logical movement by which determinations are posited through relations.

In the identity sequence, Hegel does not deny A = A. He argues that empty identity is insufficient for determinate identity. Difference develops from identity’s own requirement to be the identity of something. Diversity becomes opposition when terms determine one another. Contradiction is the result when each opposed term includes reference to what it excludes.

### Lenin and Soviet supplement

- Lenin, *Conspectus of Hegel’s Science of Logic*, selections on Essence and contradiction.
- Lenin, “On the Question of Dialectics.”
- Ilyenkov, *Dialectical Logic*, chapters treating contradiction and the relation of formal and dialectical logic.

Lenin’s language about the “division of the One” should be read as a compressed interpretation of developed relations such as identity, opposition, and contradiction. Ilyenkov is useful for explaining why dialectical contradiction is not permission to abandon determinate thought.

### Principal caution

Do not identify contradiction with any disagreement, inconsistency, social conflict, or binary opposition. A dialectical contradiction requires opposed determinations that belong to one relation, presuppose each other, and undermine their claims to independent self-subsistence.

---

chunks.title: Guide to Module 8 — Ground, Appearance, and Actuality
Guide to Module 9 — The Concept
chunks.bodyMarkdown:
### Core Hegel reading

- *Encyclopaedia Logic*, §§160–165.
- *Science of Logic*, Doctrine of the Concept:
  - Introduction to the Subjective Concept;
  - The Concept as such;
  - Universality;
  - Particularity;
  - Singularity.

### Reading focus

The transition from Essence to Concept is the transition from reciprocal necessity to self-determination. In Essence, determinations are bound through presupposed relations. In the Concept, the unity differentiates itself and remains itself in those differences.

The Concept is not an image or mental label. It is the structured unity of universal, particular, and singular. The universal is not obtained only by omitting differences among cases. It is capable of particularisation. The particular is the universal in determinate form. The singular is their concrete unity.

This sequence is foundational for later Marxist theory. The “concrete universal” cannot be reduced to a broad generalisation, and the singular cannot be reduced to an isolated atom. Yet direct applications to society belong to later courses.

### Ilyenkov supplement

- Ilyenkov, *The Dialectics of the Abstract and the Concrete in Marx’s Capital*, chapters on the universal and individual, the concrete as unity of diverse determinations, and the distinction between a concept and an abstract common feature.
- Ilyenkov, *Dialectical Logic*, selected chapters on the Concept.

Ilyenkov is especially useful here because he attacks the view that the universal is only a feature repeated across many individuals. His materialist argument should be distinguished from Hegel’s own presentation while preserving the conceptual continuity.

### Principal caution

Do not use “concrete universal” as a grand synonym for “whole.” The relation among universality, particularity, and singularity must be specified.

---

chunks.title: Guide to Module 10 — Judgment and Syllogism
Guide to Module 11 — Objectivity
chunks.bodyMarkdown:
### Core Hegel reading

- *Encyclopaedia Logic*, §§194–212.
- *Science of Logic*, Doctrine of the Concept, section on Objectivity:
  - Mechanism;
  - Chemism;
  - Teleology;
  - Subjective Purpose;
  - Means;
  - Realised Purpose.

### Reading focus

Mechanism, chemism, and teleology are logical forms of objective relation. They are not a simple chronology of scientific theories.

Mechanism treats objects as relatively indifferent units in external relation. Determinate and absolute mechanism introduce centres and laws, showing that even mechanical systems require organisation.

Chemism makes relation internal to the object’s affinity. The interacting terms are transformed through their relation.

Teleology makes the Concept explicit as purpose. External purpose imposes form upon indifferent material. Means mediate the purpose through objective laws. Realised and immanent purpose overcome the purely external relation.

### Reading caution

Hegel’s use of chemical and biological examples reflects nineteenth-century science. Preserve the logical structure while checking empirical claims against present knowledge. The categories should not be treated as competitors to contemporary physics, chemistry, or biology.

### Principal caution

Do not interpret teleology as proof that every event was planned or that history obeys a secret intention. The logical category concerns the relation of purpose, means, and objectivity.

---

chunks.title: Guide to Module 12 — The Idea and Method
chunks.bodyMarkdown:
### Core Hegel reading

- *Encyclopaedia Logic*, §§213–244.
- *Science of Logic*, Doctrine of the Concept, section on the Idea:
  - The Idea;
  - Life;
  - The Idea of Cognition;
  - The Idea of the True;
  - The Idea of the Good;
  - The Absolute Idea.

### Reading focus

The Idea is the unity of Concept and objectivity. Avoid the ordinary meaning of a thought in someone’s head.

Life is immediate self-organising unity. The living individual differentiates itself into parts and maintains itself through exchange with an environment. The genus exists through individuals and exceeds their finite lives.

Cognition divides subject and object. The theoretical Idea seeks truth; the practical Idea seeks to realise the good. Each is one-sided in isolation. Their unity is the absolute Idea.

The absolute Idea’s distinctive content is method. The logical process comprehends itself as the movement from abstract beginning through determinate negation to concrete unity. The end returns to immediacy, but it is now mediated and comprehended.

### Lenin supplement

- Lenin, *Conspectus of Hegel’s Science of Logic*, entries on the Idea and method.
- Lenin, “Plan of Hegel’s Dialectics (Logic).”

Lenin famously stresses the practical and active dimensions of cognition. Read these remarks beside Hegel’s relation of theoretical and practical Idea rather than as isolated political aphorisms.

### Principal caution

The absolute Idea is not a supernatural mind that arbitrarily creates the world. Interpretations of Hegel’s absolute idealism remain disputed, but the text at minimum presents the completed unity of logical form, objectivity, and method.

---

readingGuides.title: PHI211 Study and Reading Guide
readingGuides.workTitle: Marx's Dialectical Method: From the Critique of Hegel to the Critique of Political Economy
readingGuides.editionNote: See the guide's edition and citation policy.
readingGuides.purpose: Course reading sequence, source hierarchy, edition policy, and module-specific reading guidance.
readingGuides.context: This record references the canonical combined Study and Reading Guide without duplicating it.

chunks.title: Guide to Module 1 - The Inversion Problem
chunks.bodyMarkdown:
### Required primary reading

- Marx, Afterword to the second German edition of *Capital*, especially the discussion of inquiry, presentation, Hegel, mystification, and the rational kernel.
- Marx, Letter to Ludwig Kugelmann, 6 March 1868, on the method and the value-form.
- Hegel, *Science of Logic*, final chapter on the Absolute Idea, selectively, to recall the Hegelian account of method.

### Reading focus

Separate four claims in the Afterword:

1. inquiry differs from presentation;
2. Marx's method differs from Hegel's;
3. Hegel's dialectic is mystified;
4. Hegel nevertheless presented forms of movement comprehensively.

Do not turn the phrase "direct opposite" into a complete theory. Ask what changes when the object becomes capitalist social relations rather than the Idea.

### Principal caution

Marx says Hegel's dialectic is standing on its head and must be turned right side up. Marx is not proposing that Hegel was upright and should be placed upside down.

chunks.title: Guide to Module 2 - The 1843 Political Critique
chunks.bodyMarkdown:
### Required primary reading

- Marx, *Critique of Hegel's Philosophy of Right*, selections on family, civil society, state, monarchy, bureaucracy, and estates.
- Marx, "Introduction" to the critique, written 1843-44.
- Marx, "On the Jewish Question," selectively, on political and human emancipation.
- Hegel, *Philosophy of Right*, the paragraphs Marx comments upon.

### Reading focus

Create parallel notes:

| Hegel's claim | Marx's criticism |
|---|---|
| The state as actuality of ethical Idea | Actual social relations must explain political form |
| Mediation of particular and universal | Does the institution actually perform the mediation? |
| Estates and representation | Does representation overcome or reproduce particular interests? |

### Principal caution

The manuscript is unfinished. Do not make every polemical formulation into mature Marx's final theory of the state.

chunks.title: Guide to Module 3 - Feuerbach and Practice
Guide to Module 4 - Alienated Labour
chunks.bodyMarkdown:
### Required primary reading

- Marx, 1844 Manuscripts: "Estranged Labour," "Private Property and Communism," and the critique of Hegelian dialectic.
- Hegel, *Phenomenology of Spirit*, selected passages on objectification, labour, and alienation, with scholarly guidance.

### Reading focus

Distinguish objectification from alienation. For every form of alienation, identify the social relation that produces it. Note which terms continue into mature Marx and which are replaced by more specific categories.

### Principal caution

The 1844 manuscripts were not a finished book. Do not use an edited thematic heading as evidence that Marx had completed a stable system.

chunks.title: Guide to Module 5 - Real Individuals and Social Relations
chunks.bodyMarkdown:
### Required primary reading

- Marx and Engels, *The German Ideology*, Part I, with attention to manuscript and editorial history.
- Marx, *Theses on Feuerbach*, revisited.
- Marx and Engels, *The Holy Family*, selected passages.

### Reading focus

Ask what "real" adds to "individuals." Record the material conditions, relations, and activities through which individuality is formed. Distinguish production of means of life from a narrow factory definition of production.

### Principal caution

The familiar continuous text of *The German Ideology* is an editorial construction from manuscripts. Use it as an important source, not as a book Marx and Engels published in that form.

chunks.title: Guide to Module 6 - Historically Specific Categories
chunks.bodyMarkdown:
### Required primary reading

- Marx, 1859 Preface to *A Contribution to the Critique of Political Economy*.
- Marx, *The Poverty of Philosophy*, selections on economic categories and historical relations.
- Marx, *Wage Labour and Capital*, with attention to later editorial changes.

### Reading focus

For each category ask:

- What material process exists across societies?
- What social form is specific to capitalism?
- What makes the abstraction objectively valid?

### Principal caution

Do not treat the 1859 Preface as a mechanical diagram in which an economic base causes every legal, political, and cultural event directly.

chunks.title: Guide to Module 7 - The 1857 Introduction
chunks.bodyMarkdown:
### Required primary reading

- Marx, 1857 Introduction to the *Grundrisse*, especially "The Method of Political Economy."
- Marx, opening sections on production, distribution, exchange, and consumption.

### Reading focus

Draw two arrows:

1. represented concrete -> analytical abstractions;
2. abstract determinations -> thought-concrete.

Keep the real concrete outside both arrows as the presupposed object that thought appropriates.

### Principal caution

The ascent from abstract to concrete is a method of conceptual reproduction. It is not the historical creation of society by thought.

chunks.title: Guide to Module 8 - Inquiry and Presentation
chunks.bodyMarkdown:
### Required primary reading

- Marx, 1873 Afterword, read again.
- Marx's letters to Kugelmann and Engels concerning *Capital*, selected.
- *Capital* Volume I, Preface to the first edition, on the difficulty of analysing the commodity form.
- MEGA editorial materials on Marx's economic manuscripts, where available.

### Reading focus

Compare Marx's research archive with the polished order of *Capital*. Identify which later categories are temporarily bracketed in the opening chapters.

### Principal caution

The appearance of a priori construction is an effect of successful presentation, not evidence that empirical inquiry was unnecessary.

chunks.title: Guide to Module 9 - The Commodity
chunks.bodyMarkdown:
### Required primary reading

- *Capital* Volume I, Chapter 1, sections 1 and 2.
- *A Contribution to the Critique of Political Economy*, opening chapter, selectively.
- Marx's Notes on Adolph Wagner, selectively, for warnings against beginning from "concepts" of value detached from the commodity.

### Reading focus

Construct a distinction table:

| Term | Question answered |
|---|---|
| Use-value | What useful property or effect does the product have? |
| Exchange-value | In what quantitative relation does value appear? |
| Value | What social relation of labour is expressed? |
| Concrete labour | What specific use-value-producing activity? |
| Abstract labour | How does the labour count as part of homogeneous social labour? |
| Socially necessary labour time | Under what average social conditions is value magnitude determined? |

### Principal caution

Abstract labour is not a second kind of physical exertion hiding inside concrete labour.

chunks.title: Guide to Module 10 - Value-Form and Money
chunks.bodyMarkdown:
### Required primary reading

- *Capital* Volume I, Chapter 1, section 3.
- Marx, 1867 Appendix "The Value-Form."
- First-edition Chapter 1 where available, compared with the second edition.
- *Capital* Volume I, Chapters 2-3, selectively.

### Reading focus

Write every value-form with the roles labelled. The relative and equivalent forms are not interchangeable positions in the same expression. Track the specific defect that moves each form forward.

### Principal caution

Do not read the four forms as a literal universal chronology. They are a systematic development of value-expression.

chunks.title: Guide to Module 11 - Money to Capital
chunks.bodyMarkdown:
### Required primary reading

- *Capital* Volume I, Chapters 4-7.
- Results of the Immediate Process of Production, selections on formal and real subsumption.
- *Grundrisse*, "The Chapter on Capital," selected passages.

### Reading focus

Track the circuits C-M-C and M-C-M'. Then reconstruct the contradiction of the general formula and its solution through labour-power. Distinguish labour process from valorisation process.

### Principal caution

"Self-moving value" names an objective social inversion. It does not mean that value is literally a conscious metaphysical subject.

chunks.title: Guide to Module 12 - Fetishism and Appearance
chunks.bodyMarkdown:
### Required primary reading

- *Capital* Volume I, Chapter 1, section 4.
- *Capital* Volume I, chapter on the transformation of the value of labour-power into wages.
- *Capital* Volume III, chapters on cost price and profit, interest-bearing capital, and the Trinity Formula.

### Reading focus

For each surface form identify:

1. what participants actually experience;
2. the underlying relation;
3. the practice that generates the appearance;
4. why the appearance remains effective after theoretical criticism.

### Principal caution

Fetishism is not simply false consciousness and not a synonym for consumer culture.

chunks.title: Guide to Module 13 - Contradiction and Reproduction
chunks.bodyMarkdown:
### Required primary reading

- *Capital* Volume I, selections on commodity contradiction, the working day, machinery, and accumulation.
- *Capital* Volume II, selections on circuits and reproduction.
- *Capital* Volume III, selections on profit-rate tendencies, credit, and crisis.

### Reading focus

Do not gather quotations containing the word contradiction and assume they form one theory. Classify each relation by level: commodity, production, circulation, individual capital, total social capital, or world market.

### Principal caution

Crisis is not an automatic revolutionary subject. Contradictions can be displaced, reorganised, and resolved temporarily through destructive means.

chunks.title: Guide to Module 14 - Interpretive Traditions
chunks.bodyMarkdown:
### Required primary and reception reading

- Engels, *Anti-Duehring* and *Dialectics of Nature*, selected methodological passages.
- Lenin, *Philosophical Notebooks*, selections on Hegel and *Capital*.
- Rubin, *Essays on Marx's Theory of Value*.
- Ilyenkov, *The Dialectics of the Abstract and the Concrete in Marx's Capital*.
- Rosdolsky, *The Making of Marx's Capital*.
- Althusser and Balibar, *Reading Capital*, selected.
- representative value-form, Neue Marx-Lektuere, and systematic-dialectical works.

### Reading focus

Use an interpretation matrix:

| Tradition | Central object | View of Hegel | Strongest contribution | Principal risk |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Engelsian codification | Nature, history, thought | General dialectical laws | Broad process orientation | Excessive generality |
| Lenin's notebooks | Logic and revolutionary Marxism | Necessary for *Capital* | Recovery of mediation and contradiction | Aphorisms treated as finished doctrine |
| Rubin | Social form of labour | Indirect/form-theoretical | Value and fetishism | Exchange overemphasis in some readings |
| Ilyenkov | Concrete universal and ascent | Transformative continuity | Elementary form and totality | Philosophical reconstruction attributed directly to Marx |
| Althusser | Scientific problematic | Break and transformation | Attention to conceptual discontinuity | Rigid rupture |
| Value-form/NML | Monetary social form | Critical reconstruction | Value-form and fetishism | Production/class struggle underplayed in some variants |
| Systematic dialectics | Ordered reproduction of forms | Structural affinity | Architecture of presentation | Closed-system tendency |

### Principal caution

A later interpretation may be philosophically illuminating without being a sentence Marx himself wrote.

---

exercises.promptMarkdown: Choose one Kantian antinomy named in the section. Reconstruct it without deciding immediately which side is true.
exercises.title: Anatomy Of An Antinomy
instructions: State the thesis in one precise sentence.
State the antithesis in one precise sentence.
Identify the shared assumption that allows both arguments to arise.
Explain Kant's strategy for resolving the conflict.
Explain, in your own words, why Hegel regards Kant's discovery as profound but his restriction of contradiction as insufficient.
exercises.recommendedResponse: 350-500 words or a five-row analytical table.
exercises.solutionMarkdown: Model guidance. A successful reconstruction separates thesis and antithesis, identifies their shared treatment of the world as a completed totality, explains Kant's appearance/ thing-in-itself restriction, and then states Hegel's objection that contradiction belongs to finite determinations rather than only to misuse by a subject.

exercises.promptMarkdown: Construct a comparative map of the prehistory developed in this module.
exercises.title: From Refutation To Immanent Development
instructions: Use the rows Socrates, Plato, Aristotle, Kant, Fichte, Schelling, and Hegel.
For each row identify: the role of opposition, the status of contradiction, the usual result of dialectical movement, and the limitation Hegel identifies or inherits.
Conclude with a paragraph explaining what is specifically new in Hegel's claim that the movement belongs to the content itself.
exercises.solutionMarkdown: Model guidance. The map should show a movement from refutation and aporia, through systematic antinomies and activity, to Hegel's claim of immanent category development. It must avoid presenting the history as a simple linear accumulation.

exercises.promptMarkdown: Evaluate four proposed beginnings for logic: God, matter, the thinking I, and pure Being.
exercises.title: Testing Candidate Beginnings
instructions: For each candidate list the determinations it already presupposes.
Explain why a beginning that contains rich content may be philosophically question-begging.
State why pure Being is selected as the attempted beginning without treating it as a mysterious object.
Identify one objection to presuppositionlessness and formulate the strongest reply available from the course.
exercises.solutionMarkdown: Model guidance. God, matter, and the I already presuppose rich determinations. Pure Being is selected because it attempts minimum determinacy. The best objection notes that language and the project of logic may themselves be presupposed; the reply distinguishes methodological abstraction from an absolute absence of historical presuppositions.

exercises.promptMarkdown: Distinguish an externally imposed sequence from an internally necessary transition.
exercises.title: Internal Necessity
instructions: Give one example of an external classification in which categories could be reordered without changing their content.
Give one example from Modules 1-2 in which the next determination is constrained by a failure in the preceding one.
State the evidence required before calling a transition necessary.
Explain why necessity in Hegel is not equivalent to chronological inevitability or physical compulsion.
exercises.solutionMarkdown: Model guidance. External sequences are taxonomies whose order is imposed. Internal necessity requires a precisely defined category, an insufficiency arising from its content, and a successor that answers that insufficiency while preserving determinate content.

exercises.promptMarkdown: Analyse the difference between merely denying a claim and deriving a determinate successor.
exercises.title: Empty And Determinate Negation
instructions: Write one example of empty negation: 'not-X' without further content.
Rewrite it as a determinate negation by showing what feature of X fails and what the successor must preserve.
Identify what is retained, what is cancelled, and what is transformed.
Explain why not every criticism produces a dialectical transition.
exercises.solutionMarkdown: Model guidance. Empty negation merely says not-X. Determinate negation identifies why X cannot remain what it claims to be and therefore specifies the content the successor must include. Cancellation, preservation, and transformation should all be visible.

exercises.promptMarkdown: Select one determination already discussed in the course and reconstruct the three moments of the logical.
exercises.title: Reconstructing The Three Moments
instructions: Understanding: state the determination clearly and grant it temporary fixity.
Dialectical reason: show the limit or self-relation that destabilises it.
Speculative reason: formulate the affirmative result without erasing the distinction.
Audit your reconstruction for the thesis-antithesis-synthesis caricature, compromise thinking, and externally invented opposites.
exercises.solutionMarkdown: Model guidance. The three moments should remain moments of one content. The speculative result cannot be a compromise or arbitrary third term; it must make the opposition intelligible in a richer determination.

exercises.promptMarkdown: Reconstruct the movement Being -> Nothing -> Becoming as an argument rather than a memorised sequence.
exercises.title: The Opening Transition
instructions: Define pure Being at the stipulated level of abstraction.
Explain why no determinate content can be found in it.
Define pure Nothing without using images of empty space or destruction.
Explain the claim of indistinguishability and the simultaneous claim of difference.
Explain why Becoming expresses the instability of the two moments rather than combining two independently stable things.
exercises.solutionMarkdown: Model guidance. The reconstruction must keep Being and Nothing at the level of pure indeterminacy. Their indistinguishability and difference are moments of a movement, not claims about ordinary existing things. Becoming is that movement, not a container holding two stable objects.

exercises.promptMarkdown: Evaluate four possible readings of the opening.
exercises.title: Misreading Audit
instructions: 'Something exists, therefore nothing exists.' 'Being and Nothing are interchangeable words.' 'Hegel has proved that every opposition is identical.' 'The opening analyses the failure of pure indeterminate immediacy to remain fixed.' For each reading, mark defensible, partly defensible, or mistaken and justify the judgment in 80-120 words.
exercises.solutionMarkdown: Model guidance. Only the fourth reading is fully defensible. The first imports existential propositions, the second reduces logic to vocabulary, and the third illicitly generalises the opening to all oppositions.

exercises.promptMarkdown: Draw a relational diagram showing how Something is constituted through its relation to an Other.
exercises.title: Something, Other, And Limit
instructions: Label determination, constitution, otherness, limit, and alteration.
Show why the limit both belongs to the Something and relates it beyond itself.
Explain why a purely external boundary would not yet express Hegel's point.
Add a 250-word commentary distinguishing logical constitution from a merely spatial border.
Deliverable: diagram plus commentary.
exercises.solutionMarkdown: Model guidance. The diagram should make limit constitutive: Something is determinate through excluding and relating to Other. Limit is both its own determination and the point of passage beyond itself.

exercises.promptMarkdown: Compare two models of infinity.
exercises.title: Bad Infinity And True Infinity
instructions: Represent bad infinity as an endless alternation of finite and beyond.
Represent true infinity as a relation in which the finite's self-transcendence is comprehended within the whole.
Explain why true infinity is not a very large finite quantity.
Explain why true infinity does not simply abolish finitude.
exercises.solutionMarkdown: Model guidance. Bad infinity repeats finite/beyond externally. True infinity is a self-returning relation in which the finite's going-beyond is included. It neither means endless quantity nor the disappearance of finite moments.

exercises.promptMarkdown: Classify and analyse the following: a length of five metres, a temperature of 30 degrees, a population of 50,000, and a pressure reading.
exercises.title: Forms Of Magnitude
instructions: Identify which descriptions foreground extensive or intensive magnitude.
Explain why intensive magnitude still has quantitative determinacy.
Identify where the distinction depends on the conceptual form of measurement rather than the everyday object alone.
State one danger of treating all degrees as hidden aggregates.
exercises.solutionMarkdown: Model guidance. The classification should note that extensive magnitude is represented through multiplicity and intensive magnitude as degree. The same domain can often be represented differently; the conceptual form of measurement matters.

exercises.promptMarkdown: Analyse one real process in which quantitative variation is indifferent only within a range and then alters the relevant qualitative configuration.
exercises.title: Measure Without Mechanical 'Leaps'
instructions: Define the quality being tracked.
Define the quantitative parameter and the range of relative indifference.
Identify the nodal point or interval and justify it with domain evidence.
Explain why the case does not prove that every accumulation causes a sudden leap.
State which parts are logical reconstruction and which depend on empirical science.
exercises.solutionMarkdown: Model guidance. A valid case states the quality, parameter, evidence-based range, and nodal transformation. It explicitly separates logical structure from empirical threshold determination and refuses to universalise one case.

exercises.promptMarkdown: Build a sequence from identity through difference and opposition.
exercises.title: Reflection Determinations
instructions: State abstract identity and identify what it excludes.
Show why determinate identity requires difference.
Distinguish diversity from opposition.
Explain why positive and negative are relationally constituted rather than self- sufficient labels.
Prepare the transition to contradiction without simply asserting that opposites fight.
exercises.solutionMarkdown: Model guidance. Abstract identity is empty; determinate identity includes difference. Diversity becomes opposition when terms are defined relationally as positive and negative. Contradiction appears when each claims independence while containing relation to the other.

exercises.promptMarkdown: Compare formal inconsistency with dialectical contradiction.
exercises.title: Two Senses Of Contradiction
instructions: Give one example of a formal contradiction caused by asserting P and not-P in the same respect.
Give one example of a determination whose identity depends on an opposed moment.
Explain why dialectical analysis does not license arbitrary inconsistency.
State the respects, relations, and mediations that must be specified for the second example.
exercises.solutionMarkdown: Model guidance. Formal contradiction is P and not-P in the same respect. Dialectical contradiction concerns internally related determinations. The latter requires precision and does not suspend formal standards.

exercises.promptMarkdown: Analyse a phenomenon using the distinctions formal ground, real ground, complete ground, conditions, and fact.
exercises.title: Ground, Conditions, And The Fact
instructions: Choose a phenomenon complex enough to have several conditions.
Identify an explanation that merely repeats the phenomenon in abstract words.
Identify materially relevant grounds and conditions.
Explain why neither ground without conditions nor conditions without the grounded unity are sufficient.
Avoid treating logical ground as simply an earlier event in time.
exercises.solutionMarkdown: Model guidance. The analysis should distinguish tautological formal ground, materially relevant real ground, an integrated complete ground, enabling conditions, and the fact as their realised unity. Logical ground is not merely an earlier event.

exercises.promptMarkdown: Take one historical or institutional outcome and distinguish abstract possibility, real possibility, contingency, and necessity.
exercises.title: Modal Analysis
instructions: List what is merely non-contradictory and therefore abstractly possible.
Identify the developed conditions that make an outcome really possible.
Identify contingent features that could have varied.
Explain any necessity only as the intelligible unity of developed conditions, not as fatalism.
State what evidence would falsify your modal analysis.
exercises.solutionMarkdown: Model guidance. Abstract possibility is mere non-contradiction; real possibility is supported by conditions; contingency marks conditioned variability; necessity is the intelligible unity of conditions and content, not fatalism.

exercises.promptMarkdown: Select a concept that is not merely a taxonomic label and analyse its three moments.
exercises.title: Universality, Particularity, Singularity
instructions: State the universal as a self-relating determination, not a list of shared features.
Show how the universal particularises itself into differentiated forms.
Show how the singular is the concrete unity of universal and particular.
Explain why the singular is not merely an isolated example placed under a class.
exercises.solutionMarkdown: Model guidance. The example must show a universal that differentiates itself, particulars that are determinations of it, and a singular that concretely unites both. A list of common properties is not enough.

exercises.promptMarkdown: Compare a dictionary-style representation with a conceptual account.
exercises.title: Concept Versus Representation
instructions: Choose one term from the course, such as limit, ground, life, or purpose.
Write a concise nominal definition.
Then reconstruct the internal relations that make the determination what it is.
Explain what the conceptual account adds and what it does not permit you to ignore.
exercises.solutionMarkdown: Model guidance. A nominal definition identifies usage; conceptual analysis reconstructs internal relations and development. The latter does not eliminate the need for clear definitions or empirical knowledge.

exercises.promptMarkdown: Analyse one subject-predicate claim through the major families of judgment.
exercises.title: The Development Of Judgment
instructions: Recast it as a judgment of existence.

One purposive activity that selects and organises means toward an end.

exercises.promptMarkdown: Analyse a purposive process from subjective end to realised result.

exercises.solutionMarkdown: Model guidance. A full analysis follows subjective end, object, means, causal operation, and realised result. 'Cunning' describes indirect realisation through objective processes, not a hidden world-agent.

exercises.promptMarkdown: Construct a synoptic map of the Idea.

Show how cognition reopens the distinction between subject and object.

assessments.title: Final Examination
assessments.permittedMaterials: Primary Hegel text only; no notes or secondary literature

examSections.title: Precise Distinctions
examSections.instructionsMarkdown: Answer all ten questions. Each answer should normally be 2-4 sentences.

questions.promptMarkdown: Distinguish dialectical contradiction from formal inconsistency.
Distinguish abstract universality from concrete universality.
Distinguish bad infinity from true infinity.
Distinguish existence from actuality.
Distinguish abstract possibility from real possibility.
Distinguish a nominal definition from a Concept.
Distinguish mechanism from chemism.
Distinguish the theoretical Idea from the practical Idea.
State what determinate negation preserves that empty negation does not.
State why the understanding is necessary within dialectical thought.

examSections.title: Passage Analysis
examSections.instructionsMarkdown: Answer one of B1-B2. Analyse the passage in its exact logical context. Do not treat the sentence as an isolated slogan.

questions.promptMarkdown: “Pure being and pure nothing are, therefore, the same.” Explain the level of abstraction at which this claim is made, why sameness does not erase difference, how Becoming follows, and two common misreadings of the opening.
“Essence must appear.” Explain why appearance is not merely illusion, how the claim develops from ground and existence, and how inner/outer and possibility/actuality deepen the relation.

examSections.title: Logical Reconstruction
examSections.instructionsMarkdown: Answer one of C1-C3. Present the sequence step by step, justify each transition, and state what is preserved and transformed.

questions.promptMarkdown: Reconstruct the movement Something -> Other -> Limit -> Finitude -> Bad Infinity -> True Infinity.
Reconstruct the movement Identity -> Difference -> Opposition -> Contradiction -> Ground.
Reconstruct the movement Substance -> Causality -> Reciprocity -> Concept, explaining why necessity becomes freedom.

examSections.title: Synoptic Essay
examSections.instructionsMarkdown: Answer one of D1-D4. Your essay should formulate a thesis, reconstruct relevant categories, address an objection, and distinguish Hegel's text from later interpretations.

questions.promptMarkdown: “The thesis-antithesis-synthesis formula is not merely simplified; it obscures the forms of movement that make Hegelian dialectic distinctive.” Discuss.
Compare the characteristic movement of categories in Being, Essence, and Concept. Why can one universal dialectical template not replace these differences?
Does Hegelian contradiction conflict with the principle of non- contradiction? Develop the strongest answer available from the course and assess its limits.
Explain why teleology neither abolishes mechanism nor reduces purpose to external design. How does realised purpose lead to the Idea?

# Final Examination - Native Text

M A R X I S T. I N F O U N I V E R S I T Y P R O G R A M M E PHI111 Final Examination Hegelian Dialectics I: Being, Essence, Concept PHI111 · FINAL EXAMINATION · VERSION 1.0

[2 marks] Final Examination Time allowed 180 minutes total Total marks 100 marks Course weighting 40% Permitted material Primary Hegel text only; no notes or secondary literature Instructions. Answer all questions in Section A, one question in Section B, one question in Section C, and one question in Section D. State the exact question chosen. Definitions must be conceptually precise; essays must reconstruct rather than merely name sequences. Section A - Precise Distinctions Answer all ten questions. Each answer should normally be 2-4 sentences. A1. Distinguish dialectical contradiction from formal inconsistency.

[2 marks] [2 marks] [2 marks] [2 marks] A2. Distinguish abstract universality from concrete universality. A3. Distinguish bad infinity from true infinity. A4. Distinguish existence from actuality. A5. Distinguish abstract possibility from real possibility.

[2 marks] [2 marks] [2 marks] [2 marks] A6. Distinguish a nominal definition from a Concept. A7. Distinguish mechanism from chemism. A8. Distinguish the theoretical Idea from the practical Idea. A9. State what determinate negation preserves that empty negation does not.

[2 marks] A10. State why the understanding is necessary within dialectical thought.

[20 marks] S ECTION B · 20 MARKS Passage Analysis Answer one of B1-B2. Analyse the passage in its exact logical context. Do not treat the sentence as an isolated slogan. B1 “Pure being and pure nothing are, therefore, the same.” Explain the level of abstraction at which this claim is made, why sameness does not erase difference, how Becoming follows, and two common misreadings of the opening.

[20 marks] B2 “Essence must appear.” Explain why appearance is not merely illusion, how the claim develops from ground and existence, and how inner/outer and possibility/actuality deepen the relation.

[25 marks] S ECTION C · 25 MARKS Logical Reconstruction Answer one of C1-C3. Present the sequence step by step, justify each transition, and state what is preserved and transformed. C1 Reconstruct the movement Something -> Other -> Limit -> Finitude -> Bad Infinity -> True Infinity.

[25 marks] C2 Reconstruct the movement Identity -> Difference -> Opposition -> Contradiction -> Ground.

[25 marks] C3 Reconstruct the movement Substance -> Causality -> Reciprocity -> Concept, explaining why necessity becomes freedom.

[35 marks] S ECTION D · 35 MARKS Synoptic Essay Answer one of D1-D4. Your essay should formulate a thesis, reconstruct relevant categories, address an objection, and distinguish Hegel's text from later interpretations. D1 “The thesis-antithesis-synthesis formula is not merely simplified; it obscures the forms of movement that make Hegelian dialectic distinctive.” Discuss.

[35 marks] D2 Compare the characteristic movement of categories in Being, Essence, and Concept. Why can one universal dialectical template not replace these differences?

[35 marks] D3 Does Hegelian contradiction conflict with the principle of noncontradiction? Develop the strongest answer available from the course and assess its limits.

[35 marks] D4 Explain why teleology neither abolishes mechanism nor reduces purpose to external design. How does realised purpose lead to the Idea?

glossaryTerms.definitionMarkdown: A determination isolated from the relations that give it a developed content. “Abstract” does not simply mean difficult, theoretical, or non-material.
A relation not defined by dependence upon an external other. “Absolute” does not by itself mean infinite size, perfection in an ordinary evaluative sense, or a supernatural being.
The effective unity of Essence and existence, inner and outer. It is stronger than the bare fact that something presently exists.
The developed manifestation of Essence. Appearance is not automatically false; Essence must appear.
At the logical beginning, pure indeterminate immediacy. Later forms of being have determinate content.
A determination’s relation to what is other than it. It is one moment of determinate Being.
Self-relation achieved through negation of otherness. It develops into the One, many Ones, repulsion, and attraction.
What a determination is implicitly or in its own content before that content is fully posited.
The unity of Being and Nothing as coming-to-be and ceasing-to-be.
A form of objectivity in which objects have an internal affinity for relation and are transformed through it.
Self-determining unity of universality, particularity, and singularity. It is not merely a mental image or abstract class name.
A differentiated unity containing multiple determinations in their relations. The logical concrete can be non-sensuous.
Immediate existence required for a ground to emerge as an actual fact. Ground without conditions remains formal.
The aspect of a something expressed through relation to others, contrasted provisionally with its determination.
The developed form of opposition in which each determination includes reference to what it excludes and cannot sustain independent self-subsistence.
Being with an immediate determinacy or quality; the result of Becoming.
Negation whose content is specified by the determination negated. It produces a meaningful result rather than empty Nothing.
What makes a content this rather than another. In quality, determinacy is immediately identical with being.
The negatively rational moment in which a finite determination sublates itself through its own content.
Being mediated through negativity and reflection. Essence exists through manifestation rather than as a static hidden core.
Mediated immediacy that emerges from ground and conditions in the Doctrine of Essence.
Comparison or determination performed upon an immediate content treated as independently given.
The condition of having an immanent limit and therefore bearing the possibility of ceasing to be within one’s own determination.
The explanatory unity in virtue of which something is grounded. Ground and grounded determine one another.
Unity of Concept and objectivity. Its principal forms are life, cognition, and Absolute Idea.
Self-relation that, when determinate, includes difference. Empty identity A = A is valid but insufficient as a complete account of content.
A determination presented without an explicit mediating relation. Developed immediacy can be the result of mediation.
Arising from the content and standards of the determination itself rather than imposed from outside.
In bad infinity, an endless beyond opposed to the finite. In true infinity, self-relation achieved through the negation and inclusion of finitude.
The differentiation of the Concept into subject and predicate, singular and universal.
The negation that both bounds a something and belongs to its determination.
Unity of quality and quantity; a qualitative quantum expressing the range and relation within which a thing is what it is.
A form of objectivity in which objects are primarily indifferent and externally related.
The relation or process through which a determination is what it is by means of another. Mediation does not necessarily imply a third object located between two things.
A distinguishable but non-independent aspect of a whole. Understanding, dialectic, and speculation are moments of the logical.
Determinate exclusion, limit, or otherness. It is broader than verbal denial.
At the logical beginning, pure absence of determination, not the absence of a particular object.
The Concept in the form of immediate differentiated totality, developed through mechanism, chemism, and teleology.
Difference in which each term is determined through relation to the other, as positive and negative.
The universal in a determinate form. It mediates universality and singularity.
Reflection that generates immediacy and determination as its own result.
Determinacy initially indifferent to qualitative being; developed through continuity, discreteness, quantum, and ratio.
Mutual causal relation in which terms exchange the roles of cause and effect. It is the culmination of Essence but not yet explicit self-determination.
The movement of a determination through relation to another and return into itself. It is an objective logical form, not only subjective contemplation.
Immediacy as a vanishing and posited moment within Essence. It can be translated as shine or illusory being but is not simply error.
The unity of universal and particular reflected into itself; the actual self-related Concept.
The positively rational moment that comprehends the affirmative, concrete unity contained in a dialectical dissolution.
The unity of cancelling, preserving, and elevating a determination within a more concrete form.
Mediation of singularity and universality through particularity; more broadly, the articulated structure of rational unity.
Objectivity organised through purpose, means, and realised end. Hegel distinguishes external from immanent purpose.
The necessary moment that fixes determinations and distinguishes them. It becomes one-sided when finite determinations are treated as absolutely self-subsistent.

Self-relation capable of remaining itself through particularisation; not merely a common feature abstracted from instances.

---
Labour counted as homogeneous social labour within the value relation; not a separate physical activity.
Intellectual isolation of a determination; also a real social process when practices equate qualitatively different activities or products.
A relation in which objectified human powers confront their producers as independent powers.
The form in which a relation manifests itself; not necessarily a subjective illusion.
Value engaged in a process of self-expansion through historically specific relations of production and circulation.
A level of analysis that considers determinations common to capital before forms of competition among many capitals; its exact status changes across Marx's plans.
The movement of commodities and money through exchange; a necessary moment of capital but not the source of surplus-value by itself.
A social position within relations of production, property, control, and surplus appropriation; not merely an income group.
A product or service produced for exchange, uniting use-value and value.
A unity of many determinations and relations; in thought, the result of conceptual reconstruction.
Specific useful labour producing a particular use-value.
A determinate relation in which opposed moments presuppose one another and generate movement or instability; not every difference or conflict.
Investigation of the categories and social forms of capitalist society, including their validity, appearances, limits, and historical specificity.
A later term with several traditions; not used in this course as a substitute for reconstructing Marx's actual method.
The underlying relation or process that manifests through forms of appearance; not a separate hidden world.
The quantitative relation in which the value of one commodity is expressed in another; a form of appearance of value.
The objective appearance of social relations among producers as relations among things and natural properties of things.
A social or logical role defined by a relation, such as relative value-form, equivalent form, wage-form, or profit-form.
Capital's subordination of an existing labour process without fundamental technical transformation.
Validity of a category or relation only under determinate historical conditions.
Socially produced forms of consciousness that may express real appearances while obscuring their conditions.
Criticism that develops from the claims, forms, and contradictions of its object rather than applying only an external standard.
Research that appropriates material, analyses forms of development, and traces connections.
The capacity to labour, sold as a commodity under specific historical conditions.
Order of conceptual dependence in the presentation of a developed object; not formal deduction and not identical with chronology.
In Marx, analysis beginning from objective natural and social conditions and practical activity, not merely belief in physical substance.
Instruments, machinery, buildings, land, raw materials, and other conditions used in production.
The socially valid universal equivalent and independent form of value.
An appearance generated by and effective within the underlying relation, not an accidental error.
Activity becoming objective in products, institutions, and forms; not identical with alienation.
Ordered conceptual exposition after inquiry has established the relations of the object.
Historical processes separating producers from means of production and establishing conditions of capital; not simple saving.
Valid abstraction identifying common features of material production but insufficient for historically specific forms.
Abstraction enacted through social practice, such as the equation of different labours in exchange.
Capitalist transformation of the labour process through cooperation, machinery, science, and organisation.
Conversion of commodity value and surplus-value into money through sale.
Renewal of material conditions and social relations through repeated production and circulation.
Labour time required under normal social conditions with prevailing average productivity and intensity.
Early Marx's category for universal human productive and social capacities; its relation to mature Marx is contested.
Labour performed beyond the time necessary to reproduce labour-power.
Value produced beyond the value of labour-power and appropriated by capital.
Later reconstruction emphasising an ordered movement from abstract to increasingly concrete social forms.
A structural pressure operating through countertendencies and conditions, not a guaranteed linear prediction.
Conceptual reproduction of a real totality as a unity of many determinations.
Aggregate and interrelation of individual capitals considered at the level of social reproduction.
A differentiated whole whose moments are internally related; not an assertion that everything explains everything else.
Useful quality or effect through which something satisfies a need.
Process through which advanced value returns as greater value.
Historically specific social relation in which commodity-producing labour is represented as objectified abstract social labour.
Relational form through which commodity value appears in another commodity and ultimately in money.
Form in which the value or price of labour-power appears as payment for labour.

## Purpose and outcomes

Historical differentiation; immanent critique; source discrimination

## Assignment task

Demonstrate that Hegelian dialectic emerged from definite philosophical problems rather than from the formula thesisantithesis-synthesis. Your dossier must compare methods, objects, forms of contradiction, and outcomes. At least one section must analyse Kant's antinomies and Hegel's response.

## Required deliverables

A comparative matrix covering Socrates, Plato, Aristotle, Kant, Fichte, Schelling, and Hegel. Textual reconstruction; level-of-abstraction control; interpretive judgment

System mapping; oral explanation; distinction among logical transitions

A 3 - AFTER MODULE 5 From Human Essence to Social Relations Portfolio Weight 10% Expected extent 2,500-3,000 words across three linked pieces Mode Textual portfolio Course stage After Module 5 Task Trace one conceptual transformation from the 1844 Manuscripts through the Theses on Feuerbach to The German Ideology manuscripts. Choose alienation, human essence, labour, objectification, or social power. Argue for continuity, rupture, or determinate transformation while preserving differences of date, genre, and publication status.

## Required deliverables

Piece I: 800-1,000 word 1844 analysis. Piece II: 600-800 word Feuerbach transition. Piece III: 900-1,100 word social-relations reconstruction. A one-page continuity/rupture evidence matrix.

## Analytic rubric

Dimension Share Excellent performance Historical development rather than quotation collage 20% Accurate, complete, sourcecontrolled, and analytically independent. 1. 2. 3. 4. FORMAL ASSIGNMENTS - VERSION 1.0 Dimension Share Excellent performance Conceptual precision 20% Accurate, complete, sourcecontrolled, and analytically independent. Manuscript and edition control 20% Accurate, complete, sourcecontrolled, and analytically independent. Strength of thesis and counterargument 20% Accurate, complete, sourcecontrolled, and analytically independent. Integration of the three pieces 20% Accurate, complete, sourcecontrolled, and analytically independent.

## Pre-submission audit

Have you identified the exact text, date, and status of every central source? Have you reconstructed the relation rather than merely named it dialectical? Have you distinguished historical conditions from conceptual order? Have you stated the limits of your conclusion? • • • • FORMAL ASSIGNMENTS - VERSION 1.0

assignments.title: Abstract-to-Concrete Research Design
assignments.bodyMarkdown:
A 4 - AFTER MODULE 8 Abstract-to-Concrete Research Design Weight 12% Expected extent 2,400-2,800 words plus 8-10 minute defence Mode Research design + oral defence Course stage After Module 8 Task Design a Marxian inquiry and presentation for one complex object: housing, platform labour, healthcare markets, logistics, university commodification, energy, or another approved case. Begin from the immediate represented concrete, identify the abstractions required for inquiry, and design an ordered ascent to a thought-concrete. Distinguish conceptual dependence, historical genesis, and current reproduction.

## Required deliverables

A research archive plan identifying sources and empirical materials. A category map with at least ten determinations. A proposed order of presentation and reasons for each transition. An 8-10 minute oral defence, or a 1,500-word accessible alternative.

assignments.title: Value-Form Reconstruction and Oral Defence
assignments.bodyMarkdown:
A 5 - AFTER MODULE 10 Value-Form Reconstruction and Oral Defence Weight 10% Expected extent 2,000-2,400 words plus annotated forms Mode Technical reconstruction + oral defence Course stage After Module 10 Task Reconstruct the movement from the elementary value-form to the money-form. Explain relative and equivalent form, the defects of each stage, the social polarity of the general form, and the fetish character of the equivalent. Defend why the sequence is immanent but not a literal chronology.

## Required deliverables

Four correctly formatted and annotated value expressions. A stepwise reconstruction in no more than twelve transitions. A 900-1,100 word analysis of equivalent-form fetishism. A 10-minute oral defence or 1,500-word accessible alternative answering objections.

assignments.title: Marxological Method Research Paper
assignments.bodyMarkdown:
A 6 - AFTER MODULE 14 Marxological Method Research Paper Weight 10% Expected extent 3,500-4,500 words Mode Independent research paper Course stage After Module 14 Task Investigate one disputed question in Marx’s dialectical method. Options include Hegelian architecture of Chapter 1, abstract labour and exchange, alienation and mature Marx, logic and history, fetishism and necessary appearance, Engels’s codification, Lenin’s notebooks, Rubin, Ilyenkov, Althusser, systematic dialectics, or Neue Marx-Lektuere. The paper must compare at least two serious interpretations and adjudicate them through primary texts and editorial history.

## Required deliverables

Abstract of 150-200 words. Research question and defensible thesis. Primary-text section using at least three distinct Marx sources or versions. Comparative section engaging at least five scholarly sources. Conclusion stating confidence, limits, and unresolved evidence. 1. 2. 3. 4. 5. FORMAL ASSIGNMENTS - VERSION 1.0

## Analytic rubric

Dimension Share Excellent performance Original and answerable research question 20% Accurate, complete, source-controlled, and analytically independent. Primary-source and Marxological control 20% Accurate, complete, source-controlled, and analytically independent. Fair reconstruction of rival interpretations 20% Accurate, complete, source-controlled, and analytically independent. Independent argument and judgment 20% Accurate, complete, source-controlled, and analytically independent. Citation, structure, and academic prose 20% Accurate, complete, source-controlled, and analytically independent.

## Pre-submission audit

Have you identified the exact text, date, and status of every central source? Have you reconstructed the relation rather than merely named it dialectical? Have you distinguished historical conditions from conceptual order? Have you stated the limits of your conclusion? • • • • FORMAL ASSIGNMENTS - VERSION 1.0

## OVERALL RESULT

Assignment Performance Bands Band Standard 90-100 Exceptional primary-source command, reconstruction, and independent Marxological judgment. 80-89 Excellent, precise, well researched, and methodologically self-conscious. 70-79 Very good work with minor gaps or underdeveloped objections. 60-69 Competent reconstruction but uneven source or methodological control. 50-59 Minimum pass; substantial simplification, but core distinctions are present. Below 50 Insufficient textual evidence, confused levels of analysis, or unsupported claims. FORMAL ASSIGNMENTS - VERSION 1.0
